title: Rawalpindi fights two battleships

facts.text: Rawalpindi was a P&O passenger liner built in 1925. Requisitioned as the war began, she became an armed merchant cruiser with eight old 6 inch guns.
Her captain was Edward Coverley Kennedy, 60, a retired Royal Navy officer recalled for the war.
On 23 November 1939 she was on Northern Patrol north of the Faroe Islands, watching for German ships trying to break out into the Atlantic.
At 16:07 her lookouts sighted a ship. It was the German battleship Scharnhorst, and her sister Gneisenau was close by.
The Germans signalled her to stop. Kennedy, hopelessly outgunned, chose to fight. He was heard to say: "We'll fight them both, they'll sink us, and that will be that. Goodbye."
Kennedy had an enemy sighting report sent by radio before the shooting started.
Scharnhorst opened fire at 17:03 and hit Rawalpindi within minutes; Gneisenau joined in. Rawalpindi scored one hit on Scharnhorst, causing only splinter damage.
Kennedy was killed with more than 230 of his crew. The German ships picked up survivors, and the cruiser HMS Chitral later found 11 more.
Kennedy was mentioned in dispatches after his death.
His son Ludovic, then a young naval officer, served in the destroyer HMS Tartar in the hunt for the Bismarck in 1941 and later became a well known broadcaster and author.
In 1971 Ludovic Kennedy made a BBC television series, The Life and Death of the Scharnhorst, which brought him face to face with survivors of the ship that sank his father's.

declassified.fact: Rawalpindi's report named her attacker as the pocket battleship Deutschland. The British were still hunting for Deutschland as Scharnhorst and Gneisenau slipped home to Germany.
